en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, First Part, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master and Dharma-Transmitting Grand Master Shi Hu,
who was granted the purple robe by imperial decree, during the Western Heaven (India).
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where the elder Kāśyapa of Uruvilvā was staying,
and having arrived there, Kāśyapa saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, approaching from afar, and immediately addressed the Buddha,
saying: "Welcome, Great Śramaṇa!"
"Whatever clothing, food, or drink you may require, I shall provide it all for you.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa,
"I shall now stay overnight in this house of yours."
Kāśyapa replied, "This house is not my dwelling; it is my fire-chamber.
A great nāga resides within it, possessing great supernormal powers and immense majesty. If you were to stay there now, I fear he might harm you."
Thereupon, for a second and third time, the World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa:
"Let me simply stay for one night within this assembly."
Then Kāśyapa also addressed the Buddha a second and a third time, saying:
"A great dragon dwells therein; I fear he may cause you harm. You should now trust and accept my words."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I should not speak many words to him now, for I have given rise to a heart of compassion and am determined to turn [him] away."
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered the fire-hall, folded his saṃghāṭī robe into four layers, placed it upon the clean grass, and then the World-Honored One sat down cross-legged.
At that time, the dragon conceived a mind of malice and spat forth smoke and flames, filling his house.
The World-Honored One immediately entered the fire-element samādhi and likewise emitted smoke and flames that surrounded the house, until it became entirely a single mass of blazing, fierce fire.
That nāga further emitted great, fierce flames of various colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—and the World-Honored One likewise emitted flames of various colors—blue, yellow, red, and white.
At that time, the elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, together with his own retinue, circumambulated the fire-hut and spoke these words:
"This great śramaṇa possesses the most excellent physical marks; since he did not heed my words beforehand, he will surely be harmed by the nāga."
At that time, by the power of his supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), the World-Honored One caused the dragon’s majestic radiance to be naturally withdrawn in an instant.

Then Kāśyapa, knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had likewise attained supernatural powers, spent the remainder of the night observing as the Buddha manifested various miracles according to what was appropriate. He then went to investigate and saw that the dragon’s majestic radiance was gradually diminishing, while the light of the World-Honored One grew ever more intense and blazing.
At that time, at dawn, the World-Honored One subdued that nāga, placed it within his alms bowl, and holding it up for Kāśyapa to see, said:
"This is the nāga from the fire-hut whom I have subdued."
“Kāśyapa! This nāga possesses great power; ordinary worldlings cannot enter his abode.
At that time, Kāśyapa was struck with wonder and gave rise to pure faith.
"How can my mind of renunciation be stopped!
Furthermore, at the first part of the day, the elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, wishing to perform the fire-sacrifice ritual, had this thought:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great majesty and is endowed with great supernormal powers; he has even the power to subdue dragons of great majesty."
"I shall now perform the fire-ritual during the first watch of the day; that great śramaṇa should perform his miraculous feat during the last watch of the day."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Kāśyapa had faith in the Buddha’s supernormal powers, immediately withdrew his supernormal power. Having accomplished his great task during the first part of the day, Kāśyapa was struck with wonder and gave rise to pure faith, thinking:
"How could my resolve for the homeless life ever be turned back!"
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, wishing to perform the fire-ritual during the afternoon, had this thought:
"This great śramaṇa possesses great majesty and great supernormal powers; he has even the power to subdue dragons of great majesty. I shall now simply perform the fire-ritual during the afternoon."
"That great śramaṇa should perform a feat of supernatural power during the first part of the day.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Kāśyapa had faith in the Buddha’s supernatural powers, immediately withdrew his supernormal power.
Then, during the latter part of the day, after Kāśyapa had accomplished his great task, he was filled with wonder and gave rise to pure faith, thinking:
"How could my aspiration for the homeless life ever be restrained!"

Furthermore, Kāśyapa employed various other methods for kindling fire, yet none succeeded; he even threw dry wood into it, as well as dry grass, dry *gomaya*, clarified butter, oil, and other such substances.
He threw everything that was to be used into it; then, manifesting an unwholesome appearance, he uttered these incantations:
“Ilisaka! Talisaka! Everything can be burned—why does this not burn?”
Having uttered this incantation, the fire still would not burn.
Then Kāśyapa thought to himself:

"This great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and great majestic authority; he has such great majestic authority that he can even subdue a dragon. With what object should I make an offering to him?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Kāśyapa had faith in the Buddha’s supernormal powers, immediately exercised his own supernormal power so that the fire would ignite.
Then Kāśyapa was struck with wonder and gave rise to pure faith, thinking:
"How could my intention to leave the household life ever be thwarted!"

Furthermore, after Kāśyapa had performed the ritual, he wished to extinguish the fire; yet despite his various efforts, he could not put it out. He then took pure earth and scattered it into the flames, followed by throwing ashes and sprinkling water.
Seeing that these were ineffective, he uttered these incantations with an air of displeasure: “Ilisaka! Talisaka! Everything has been burned; why does this not go out?”
Having uttered this incantation, the fire still did not go out. Then Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and great majesty; he has even the power to subdue a dragon of such great majesty. With what thing should I make an offering to him?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Kāśyapa had faith in the Buddha’s supernormal powers, immediately withdrew his supernormal power, whereupon the fire was extinguished.
Then Kāśyapa, filled with wonder and admiration, gave rise to pure faith, thinking:
"How could my intention to leave the household life ever be stopped!"

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, while he was taking a brief nap during the daytime, the World-Honored One immediately manifested five hundred elders whose appearances were identical to Kāśyapa’s, and they all went to his location.
When the transformed beings had arrived, they raised their voices and mocked one another with laughter.
Hearing this sound of laughter, Kāśyapa woke from his sleep and thought to himself:
"For what reason am I now so deeply attached to sleep?"
"We do not even know when fellow practitioners of the holy life come.
Then that transformed assembly all praised these words, saying: "Excellent!"
"Excellent!
At that time, Kāśyapa observed them all around and, seeing the physical forms of each one, thought to himself:
"Could this not be a transformation produced by the supernatural power of the Great Śramaṇa?"
"That great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and great majesty; he has even the power to subdue dragons of great majesty. With what, then, shall I make an offering to him?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Kāśyapa had gained faith in the Buddha’s supernormal powers, immediately withdrew his supernormal power, and those manifested beings suddenly vanished from sight.
At that time, Kāśyapa was filled with wonder and gave rise to pure faith, thinking:
"How could my resolve for the homeless life ever be restrained!
Then, the World-Honored One departed from Kāśyapa’s dwelling and proceeded to the bank of the Nairañjanā River, to the foot of an Ajapāla tree in the village of Koṇāgamana.
When the World-Honored One was traveling, his person was endowed with dignified deportment and his countenance was worthy of contemplation; having arrived there, he paused for a moment.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"At this very moment, we too have gone to the banks of the Nairañjanā River to perform the ritual of purification by water, and the Great Śramaṇa is also there."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went with his retinue to the banks of the Nairañjanā River. Upon arriving, he suddenly saw the water flowing upstream and thought again:
"This water flowing upstream—is this not the work of the Great Śramaṇa’s supernatural power?"
Yet this great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and great majesty, even to the point of being able to subdue dragons of great majesty; with what, then, shall I make an offering?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Kāśyapa had faith in the Buddha’s supernormal powers, withdrew his supernormal power, and the water immediately flowed downstream.
Then Kāśyapa was struck with wonder and gave rise to pure faith, thinking:
"How could my resolve for the homeless life ever be turned back?"

Furthermore, as the World-Honored One was gradually proceeding to cross the Nairañjanā River to go toward the village of Pāṭaligrāma, a great cloud suddenly arose and torrential rain poured down; the river swelled and roared with a sound like that of conch shells being blown.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded slowly through the swift current; the waters parted into two streams, and dust rose with every step.
Then Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa is now crossing the middle of the river; the water is so rapid that he will surely be swept away."

While he was reflecting thus, he beheld the World-Honored One in the midst of a swift current; the waters parted into two channels, and as the Buddha stepped forward, dust rose with every footfall until he gradually reached the shore.
He immediately gave rise to a sense of wonder and exclaimed:
"How rare and difficult to encounter!
This name of the Great Śramaṇa, I have never heard before in all the worlds."
At that time, Kāśyapa conceived pure faith, thinking:
"How could my intention to renounce the world ever be stopped!
Having witnessed such miraculous feats of the Buddha, Kāśyapa’s most supreme and pure faith was further aroused; filled with deep affection and joy, he spoke these words:
“O Great Śramaṇa Buddha!
You are able to perform such miraculous deeds; with what object should I make an offering?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having reached the other shore, came to rest within the village of Bandhumatī.
That very night, the Eastern Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra came to where the Buddha was, paid homage by bowing at his feet, and the radiance of his body shone forth with vast brilliance.
That night, having witnessed this light, Kāśyapa went to the place where the Buddha was at dawn. Upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
"Great Śramaṇa! For what reason did a vast light come from the east and illuminate the night so brightly?"

The World-Honored One replied, “The light that appeared in the east during the night was that of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King who Protects the Nation; he came to pay homage at my feet, and the radiance of his body shone forth in such a manner.”
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"We have heard his name, yet we have not been able to see him; how much less could he come to pay homage at the feet of the śramaṇa?"
"Observing this matter, it is rare and difficult to encounter," he thought,
and then gave rise to pure faith:
"How could my resolve to leave the household life ever be stopped!"

During the second watch of the night, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, Lord of the Southern Quarter, came to where the Buddha was, paid homage by prostrating at his feet; the radiance from his body shone forth with vast brilliance.
That night, having witnessed this light, Kāśyapa went to the Buddha’s dwelling at dawn. Upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
“Great Śramaṇa! For what reason did a vast light come from the south and illuminate the night?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"The light that appeared from the south during the night was that of the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, who came to prostrate at my feet; it was the radiance of his body that shone in such a manner."
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"We have heard his name, yet we have not been able to see him; how much less could he come to pay homage at the feet of the śramaṇa?"
"Observing this matter, I find it rare and difficult to encounter," he thought,
and then gave rise to pure faith:
"How could my resolve to leave the household life ever be restrained!"

During the third watch of the night, Virūpākṣa, the Deva-king of the West, came to where the Buddha was, paid homage by bowing at his feet, and the radiance of his body shone forth with vast brilliance.
That night, having witnessed this light, Kāśyapa went to the Buddha’s dwelling at dawn. Upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
“Great Śramaṇa! For what reason did a vast light come from the west and illuminate the night so brightly?”

The World-Honored One replied, “That light appearing in the west during the night was from the Heavenly King Vaishravana, who came to prostrate at my feet; it was the radiance of his body that shone in such a manner.”
At that time, Kāśyapa had this thought:
"We have heard his name, yet we have not been able to see him; how much less could he come to pay homage at the feet of the śramaṇa?"
"Observing this matter, I find it rare and difficult to encounter," he thought,
and then gave rise to pure faith:
"How could my resolve to leave the household life ever be stopped!"

During the fourth watch of the night, the Northern Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa came to where the Buddha was, paid homage by bowing at his feet, and the radiance of his body shone forth with vast brilliance.
That night, having witnessed this light, Kāśyapa went to the Buddha’s dwelling at dawn. Upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
“Great Śramaṇa! For what reason did a vast light come from the north and illuminate the night so brightly?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"That light appearing in the north during the night was that of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, who came to prostrate at my feet; it was the radiance of his body that shone in such a manner."
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"We have heard his name, yet we have not been able to see him; how much less could he come to pay homage at the feet of the śramaṇa?"
"Observing this matter, it is rare and difficult to encounter," he thought,
and then gave rise to pure faith:
"How could my resolve to leave the household life ever be halted!"

During the fifth watch of the night, Śakra, the King of Gods from the upper realm, came to where the Buddha was, paid homage by prostrating at his feet, and the radiance of his body shone forth with vast brilliance.
That night, having witnessed this light, Kāśyapa went to the Buddha’s dwelling at dawn. Upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
“Great Śramaṇa! For what reason did a vast light come from the zenith and illuminate the night so brightly?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"That light appearing above in the night was Śakra, Lord of the Devas, who came to pay homage at my feet; it was the radiance of his body that shone in such a manner."
At that time, Kāśyapa had this thought:
"We have heard his name, yet we have not been able to see him; how much less could he come to pay homage at the feet of the śramaṇa?"
"Observing this matter, it is rare and difficult to encounter," he thought,
and then gave rise to pure faith:
"How could my mind to leave the household life be restrained!"

During the sixth night, the Four Great Heavenly Kings from the four directions and Śakra, Lord of the Devas from above, together approached the Buddha’s dwelling, paid homage by prostrating at his feet, and departed. The bodily radiance of the Four Kings illuminated the four directions respectively;
the bodily radiance of Śakra shone resplendently from above.
However, all those rays were entirely withdrawn back into the light of the World-Honored One’s samādhi.
Having beheld these rays that night, Kāśyapa went to the Buddha’s dwelling at dawn; having arrived, he addressed him, saying: “Great Śramaṇa!
"Why is it that during the night light comes from the four directions, and why does light also come from above to illuminate?
The World-Honored One replied,
"The light appearing from the four directions at night is that of the Four Great Heavenly Kings."
"The light from above is that of Śakra, Lord of the Devas;
they have all come together to prostrate at his feet, and the radiance of their bodies shines forth in this manner.
At that time, Kāśyapa had this thought:
“People have come from all five directions to pay homage at the feet of the śramaṇa; observing this matter, it is rare and difficult to encounter.
Thereupon, he gave rise to pure faith and thought:
“How could my resolve to leave the household life be stopped!”
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa:
"Now, for my sake, go into the Āmalaka grove and fetch some of those fruits.
By the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, Kāśyapa immediately took them as instructed and presented them to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"Go to the Harītakī grove and bring back those medicinal herbs.
Kāśyapa did as he was told and presented them to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"From the Jambu tree, first take its fruit; next, you may also take various other fruits as they correspond to what you know."
Kāśyapa took it as he was told and offered it to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"Go to Uttarakuru and bring back some rice from there."
Kāśyapa took it as he was told and presented it to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"From among the Thirty-three Heavens, take those mandārava flowers and bring them here."
Kāśyapa took it as instructed and offered it to the Buddha.
At that time, Kāśyapa, recognizing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possessed such various supernormal powers, gave rise once again to the most supreme and pure faith.
The World-Honored One, having known his mind, again employed his supernormal powers before Kāśyapa, manifesting distinct bodily forms in mid-air and displaying three modes of deportment:
namely, the deportment of standing, the deportment of walking, and the deportment of sitting cross-legged.
All such manifested postures and characteristics were exceedingly swift, like treading upon a rapid current; these manifestations were likewise so.
Furthermore, within the sky, he manifested celestial palaces constructed from various jewels;
moreover, he universally manifested a golden-hued appearance.
After the World-Honored One had manifested these various supernatural powers, he withdrew his spiritual power, and his physical appearance returned to its original state.
At that time, Kāśyapa would regularly select one day each year at his own residence to perform a sacrificial assembly for the gods.
All the kings of Magadha, King Bimbisāra of the great city of Rājagṛha, and all the people within the kingdom came together to attend the assembly.
Then Kāśyapa, knowing that the time for the sacrificial assembly had arrived, returned to his own dwelling and thought to himself:
"The time has now come for the sacrificial assembly for the gods that I regularly perform; the king and the people have all gathered together."
That great śramaṇa has a face that is even and full; he is free from frowning, devoid of anger, and utters only virtuous speech, bringing joy to all who behold him.
"If this most excellent of virtuous men comes to my house while I am holding a sacrifice for the gods, how will I be able to perform the rites?

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, immediately manifested his supernatural power and went to Uttarakuru to beg for food as usual. Returning to the vicinity of the Snowy Mountains, he sat down to eat; having finished eating, he constructed a grass hut there and stayed overnight.
At that time, after Kāśyapa had finished his sacrifice to the gods and concluded his assembly, the food and provisions required were still abundant and overflowing.
Upon seeing this, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"If that Great Śramaṇa comes now, I shall offer him food."
The World-Honored One, knowing his thought, came through the air and appeared before him.
Upon seeing him, Kāśyapa spoke these words:
"Welcome, Great Śramaṇa!"
"I held an assembly yesterday; why did you not come?
The World-Honored One replied, "I knew that you had conceived such a thought; therefore, I did not come."
The World-Honored One then spoke to him exactly according to his thoughts.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"For what reason have you come here today?"
The World-Honored One replied, “I also know your thought; it is because you wish to offer me food that I have come here.
At that time, Kāśyapa had this thought:
"How rare and difficult to encounter!
This great śramaṇa knows my thoughts; he must surely be like me, having also attained arhatship.
The World-Honored One, knowing his reflections, immediately said to him:
“Kāśyapa! You are not an arhat, nor do you know the dharma of an arhat.
Having heard this, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
“Rare, rare indeed!
This Great Śramaṇa is able to know completely both the mind and the thought, as well as both applied thought and sustained thought.”
Having formed this thought, he prostrated with his head to the ground, approached to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I now take refuge in the Buddha, seeking to leave the household life and receive full ordination. I only pray that the Sugata will compassionately accept me.”
The Buddha said,
"Kāśyapa! You should not now seek ordination by joining the Buddha."

Why is this so? Because the King of Magadha and all his people revere, honor, and make offerings to you; among your kinsmen and acquaintances, you are the most virtuous person. You ought now to reflect deeply upon yourself.
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
“Do not say such things! Do not say such things!”

In the presence of the World-Honored One, I have conceived a heart of supreme joy and given rise to sublime love and delight; how could I possibly deliberate further? I am now determined to take refuge in the Buddha and go forth into homelessness.
For what reason?
World-Honored One!

Having gone forth, I shall, among the assemblies of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and non-Buddhists, subdue all those who revile and find fault; bearing the supreme banner, I shall walk in succession through the great city of Rājagṛha, declaring that I, the elder Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, have attained liberation within the pure Dharma of the World-Honored One. For this reason, I now resolutely take refuge in the Buddha and go forth.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and accept us.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
If you are determined to take refuge in the Buddha and go forth into homelessness, that is most excellent; however, at this time, you should also deliberate together with your own kinsmen.
At that time, Kāśyapa, following the Buddha’s instruction, consulted with his followers, saying:
"You should all know that the Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, possesses great supernormal powers and great majestic authority; all who see him give rise to joy."
"I have conceived a most supreme and pure faith in the Buddha; I am now determined to go forth into homelessness under him.
His kinsmen said, "If even our master, the Noble One, can give rise to such a light and resolute mind, how could we all not likewise go forth?"
Therefore, at this time, each of us also desires with joy to take refuge in the Buddha and leave the household life.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Part One, Volume Upper.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Part One, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master and Dharma-transmitting Grand Master Shi Hu,
recipient of the purple robe, by imperial decree. At that time,
the elder Kāśyapa of Uruvilvā, together with his five hundred followers, returned to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in homage at his crown, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now take refuge in the Buddha and go forth from the household life; I shall uphold the precepts. May the Buddha graciously accept me.”
The Buddha said, “Welcome!
You shall now practice the holy life within my Dharma.
At that moment, Kāśyapa’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord; a kāṣāya robe was draped upon his body, and he held an alms bowl, assuming the appearance of a bhikṣu.
At that time, the Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa took his hair and offered it to the World-Honored One, speaking these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"May these hairs of mine be used to wipe the Buddha’s feet; I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will accept this offering of mine.
Thus, Kāśyapa, having gone forth, his various kinsmen also each went forth.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa immediately took those former implements for fire-worship—namely, the purified grass, tiger skins, cow hides, tree bark, the three staffs, the water-purifying vessel, and the *kṛka* cleansing vessels—and cast them all away into the Nairañjanā River.

At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa was on the banks of the lower reaches of that river together with three hundred followers. Seeing the implements for fire-worship that had been cast away floating downstream to him, he thought to himself:
"Could it be that my elder brother, Uruvilvā-Kāśya, has been harmed by humans or non-humans?"
"If this were not so, why would he discard and cast away the objects he had used?
Having thought this, he immediately went with his retinue to that place.
Having arrived, he saw his elder brother and five hundred attendants together with the Buddha, all serving as bhikṣus and practicing the holy life (brahmacarya). He then spoke these words:

"My elder brother Uruvilvā, you whom this King of Magadha and his people revere, honor, and provide for with offerings—what have you seen or heard that you are now able to leave the household life and practice the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa?"
"I observe this matter and find it most rare and extraordinary.

Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa said, "The World-Honored Buddha possesses great supernormal powers and immense majesty; he is able to perform various miraculous transformations and such deeds. Having seen these signs, I have conceived pure faith and have gone forth from home to practice the Way within the Buddha’s Dharma."
"You should now likewise give rise to pure faith and go forth into homelessness under the Buddha.

At that time, having heard these words, Nadi-Kāśyapa conceived the aspiration for renunciation; he immediately went before the Buddha with his retinue, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We take refuge in the Buddha and have gone forth; we shall uphold the precepts. We pray that the Buddha will accept us.
The Buddha said, "Welcome! Now, within my Dharma, cultivate and maintain the holy life."
At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and with the saṃghāṭī robe covering his body and the alms bowl in hand, he took on the appearance of a bhikṣu.
His kinsmen likewise each went forth into the homeless life.

Furthermore, Nadi-Kāśyapa immediately took up those former implements for fire-worship—namely, the purified grass, tiger skins, ox hides, bark from fruit trees, the triple staff, the water-purifying vessel, and the *kṛka* purification vessels—and cast them all away into the Nairañjanā River.
At that time, Gayākāśyapa was also by the lower reaches of that river with two hundred followers. Seeing the implements for fire-worship cast away floating downstream, he thought to himself:
"Could it be that my elder brothers, Uruvilvākāśyapa and Nadīkāśyapa, have been harmed or afflicted by some human or non-human being?"
"If it were not so, why would he discard and cast away the items he had used?
Having thought this, he immediately went forward with his retinue, approaching step by step to inquire as to the reason.
He then saw his two elder brothers along with their retinues, all standing by the Buddha as bhikṣus, practicing the holy life (brahmacarya).
He immediately said:

"My elder brother Uruvelā, you whom this King of Magadha and his people respect, revere, and make offerings to—what have you seen or heard that you are now able to leave the household life and practice the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa?"
"I observe this matter and find it most extraordinary.

Uruvilvā Kāśyapa said, "The World-Honored Buddha possesses great supernormal powers and great majestic authority; he is able to perform various miraculous transformations and such deeds. Seeing these signs, I have given rise to pure faith and have left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha's Dharma."
"You should now likewise give rise to pure faith and go forth into homelessness under the Buddha.

At that time, having heard these words, Gayākāśyapa conceived the aspiration for renunciation; he immediately went with his retinue to where the Buddha was, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in homage, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We take refuge in the Buddha and have left the household life to uphold the precepts; we pray that the Buddha will accept us.
The Buddha said, "Welcome! Now, within my Dharma, cultivate and maintain the holy life."
At that time, Gayā-Kāśyapa’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord; a kāṣāya robe was draped upon his body and he took up an alms bowl, thus assuming the appearance of a bhikṣu.
His various kinsmen likewise each went forth into homelessness.

Furthermore, Gayākāśyapa immediately took those former implements for fire-worship—namely, the purified grass, tiger skins, cow hides, bark from fruit trees, the triple staff, the water-purifying vessel, the *karkara* water-jar, and other such cleansing utensils—and cast them all into the River Nairañjanā.
Thus, after the three Kāśyapas and their retinues had all gone forth together,
the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa addressed one person from among his followers, saying:
"Go to King Bimbisāra and speak these words on my behalf:"

Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa addressed the King, saying: "I, together with my younger brothers and their followers, have now followed the Buddha to leave the household life and cultivate the Way. As for the various offerings of faith you previously bestowed upon me, I have now returned them; I pray that Your Majesty will desist."
The messenger received his orders and immediately went to inform the king.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having converted the three Kāśyapas, proceeded together with this assembly of bhikṣus to Mount Elephant Head (Gajaśīrṣa).
Having arrived and settled there, he thought to himself:
"Although Kāśyapa’s followers are elderly and have long served the Fire God, believing in the rites of fire, they do not understand that all phenomena are impermanent; I shall now teach them this."
Having formed this thought, the World-Honored One immediately leaped up into the air and manifested a great mass of flames; thus he appeared with blazing and intense radiance.
Returning to his original seat, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know that the eye-faculty is impermanent, visual objects are impermanent, eye-consciousness is impermanent, and eye-contact is impermanent."
The feelings of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity produced with eye-contact as a condition are all impermanent.

The faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent; the objects of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are impermanent; the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent; the contacts of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent; and all feelings produced with the contacts of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as conditions are entirely impermanent.

"O Bhikṣus! The fire of greed is impermanent; the fire of hatred is impermanent; the fire of delusion is impermanent; and birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair are all entirely impermanent."
"O bhikṣus! Therefore, you should understand all phenomena (dharmas) to be impermanent in this way.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!"

You should know this: the eye-faculty is not grasped; visual objects are not grasped; eye-consciousness is not grasped; eye-contact is not grasped; and all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are entirely not grasped.

The faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not accepted; the objects of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are not accepted; the consciousnesses of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not accepted; the contacts of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not accepted; and all feelings that arise conditioned by the contact of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are entirely not accepted.
“O Bhikṣus! Because it is thus, one does not grasp at any phenomena; because of this non-grasping, one is immediately freed from dust and defilement and attains liberation.”
“Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence.
When the Buddha spoke this Dharma, sixty bhikṣus in the assembly attained liberation of mind through non-clinging to all phenomena, and the remaining bhikṣus also fully understood the Dharma.
At that time, having spoken this Dharma, the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, proceeded to Daṇḍaka Hill; upon arrival, he settled there.

The World-Honored One then manifested three kinds of supernormal powers for the bhikṣus—namely, the power of miraculous feats (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), the power of preaching the Dharma (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*), and the power of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*)—and through these supernormal powers, he demonstrated, benefited, and gladdened them.
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus! You should attend to things in this way, investigate them in this way, understand them in this way, and practice accordingly; thus you shall obtain benefit and happiness."

At that time, the bhikṣus witnessed and heard all these matters concerning the three types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Having been shown, benefited, and gladdened, those in the assembly who had attained liberation through the mind spoke this verse:
"At Mount Gajaśīrṣa and Mount Daṇḍaka, The World-Honored One preached the Dharma and manifested miraculous transformations.
He subdued the non-Buddhists and led them back to the True and Right, Causing their deviant minds to attain complete liberation."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"I now wish to enter the great city of Rājagṛha.

Then King Bimbisāra first heard that one endowed with the ten titles—Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān—had appeared in the world.

Among the great assembly of devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he attained perfect enlightenment through his own power of wisdom and proclaimed all dharmas—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; profound in both letter and meaning, pure and unadulterated, complete and immaculate, the very mark of the holy life (brahmacarya).
In that Buddha’s assembly, there were Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, and Gayā-Kāśyapa, along with their retinues, who took refuge in the Buddha, left the household life, and practiced the holy life.

Today, this Buddha, the World-Honored One, intends to enter the great city of Rājagṛha; the king immediately issued orders to repair and adorn both the interior and exterior of the royal city, ensuring that all streets, lanes, and thoroughfares were completely purified. He burned various famous incenses, scattered many exquisite flowers, hung strings of pearls and jewels, and erected banners and canopies, thus making the entire city magnificent and beautiful in every place.
Even throughout the city, all the people raised voices of joy that could be heard by one another.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, wearing new, exquisite robes and donning sandals adorned with many jewels, arrayed his fourfold army and, accompanied by countless attendants leading and following him, departed from Rājagṛha to welcome the World-Honored One.
The king, together with his retinue, departed from the city and traveled a great distance; as they drew near to the World-Honored One, the king descended from his carriage and proceeded on foot.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by his bhikṣus, both before and behind, as he entered the city of Rājagṛha.
The king and his retinue, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, welcomed him with solemn reverence and followed him into the city.
As the Buddha entered the city, the people within raised their voices in unison, reciting this verse:
“The World-Honored One enters this city of Rājagṛha, Manifesting the radiant appearance of a lion.”
"Surrounded by the assembly of elders, those liberated ones, each showing them deep respect.
At that time, King Bimbisāra led the way as the World-Honored One proceeded toward the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

Having arrived, the World-Honored One surveyed the surroundings; the king then prepared a seat for the Buddha, and once the Buddha was seated, the assembly of bhikṣus each took their places behind him.

At that time, among the king and his retinue, some prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; some merely joined their palms and bowed their heads in homage; some gave rise to a heart of joy; and some, upon giving rise to such joy, immediately conceived a sense of loving devotion. Having thus each extended their respects, they withdrew and sat to one side.

The King then rose again from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and with his right hand holding a most exquisite golden pitcher, poured forth sublime scented water to wash the hands of the World-Honored One. Having washed them, he addressed him, saying:

"I offer this grove to the World-Honored One and the Saṃgha of the four directions for their peaceful dwelling and use. This is my very first gift of a grove; I pray that the World-Honored One will graciously accept it for my sake."
The Buddha accepted [the offering] immediately.
After the king had prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he turned toward the Venerable Uruvelā Kassapa, joined his palms in joy, and spoke these words:

“Kassapa, all the people in this kingdom of Magadha revere you; I too have always respected and made offerings to you. What have you seen or heard that leads you now to go forth under the Buddha and practice the holy life?”

Kāśyapa replied: "Great King, you should know that the present Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses great supernormal powers and immense majesty; he is able to perform various miraculous transformations and such deeds. For these reasons, I have conceived pure faith and have gone forth under the Buddha."
At that time, within the assembly, there were those who conceived a doubt, thinking:
"This Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa is now practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Great Śramaṇa; what is it that he seeks?"
"This one has been able to direct his heart toward refuge, and the Buddha has been able to accept him; what signs have they seen to one another that it has come to this?
Furthermore, among the assembly, some spoke thus:
"This Uruvilvā Kāśyapa is now practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) at the side of the Great Śramaṇa; he can no longer receive the respectful offerings of King Bimbisāra."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the doubts of the assembly, addressed the Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, saying:
“Kāśya, you know the proper time; it is fitting that you now manifest your supernatural powers.”

At that time, having received the Buddha’s command, Kāśyapa entered into samādhi as was appropriate for him. Like a king of geese, he rose into the air and, by means of his supernormal powers, emitted fire from the upper part of his body and water from the lower part;
he emitted fire from the lower part of his body and water from the upper part;
he emitted fire from his right side and water from his left side.
From his left side fire issued forth, and from his right side water issued forth;
in the four directions, he manifested the postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.

Having displayed these supernormal powers, he descended from the air and stood before the Buddha. With his right shoulder bared and his right knee touching the ground, he joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself before the World-Honored One, and addressed him thus:
“The Buddha is my teacher, and I am his śrāvaka disciple. Whether I know or do not know, the Buddha knows it all; what the Buddha has realized is the supreme knowledge.”
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa!
As for the practice of fire-worship you previously performed, what purpose did you perceive in it? Did you find tranquility therein?”
"Can one who is subject to defilement act [as such]?
According to what you have done, none are liberated; now I ask about this meaning, so answer as you see fit.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Because I lacked wisdom, I did not know this before; now that the World-Honored One, the Great Naga, has skillfully delivered me, I have seen the unsurpassed state."
“World-Honored One!
What I previously practiced—providing food and drink as offerings and kindling fire to sacrifice to the heavens—was truly not liberation.

Although such food and drink may be replete with various exquisite flavors, they ultimately cannot free one from the category of the three desires. Now, having received the Buddha’s guidance, I see it thus.”
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa! Furthermore, just as the practices you perform, such as the fire-worship and other rites, are not to be cherished by gods or humans in this world.”
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I have now, within the True Dharma of the Buddha, perceived the most supreme words; abiding in a mind of tranquility, I shall ultimately never again fall into the realm of desire. I shall no longer practice within other divergent teachings; for this reason, I have abandoned such practices as the tending of sacrificial fires.”
At that time, the Venerable Nadī-Kāśyapa addressed the Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, saying:

"The Blessed One, the World-Honored One, has realized the Dharma of Nirvana; he is free from faults and untainted, supremely pure, and teaches the Dharma that transcends the world for the sake of vast benefit."
"And you, Kāśyapa, are also able to speak well.
At that time, the Venerable Gayākāśyapa spoke these verses for King Bimbisāra:
"Welcome, Great King, listen to my words: I have long dwelt upon Mount Gayā."
The Perfectly Awakened One has appeared in the world; by hearing the words of Nirvāṇa, I have gained benefit.
The Buddha, the most supreme, the Great Elephant, the Dragon, the Unsurpassed Tamer, the Most Exalted Honored One—fearless and skillfully guiding all sentient beings, his mind is tranquil in samādhi.
In the long night of the past, my mind was defiled, Giving rise to various false views from which I found no liberation;
Now the Buddha has shattered my mind of false views, And all its entanglements have completely dissolved.

At that time, the doubts of the assembled multitude were all stilled; they realized how truly rare it was that the Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, together with his followers, had gone forth from home to follow the Buddha, renouncing the world to practice the holy life.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the assembly had already stilled their doubts, proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma for King Bimbisāra and the others, following the teaching format of previous Buddhas: namely, discourse on generosity, discourse on ethical discipline, and discourse on rebirth in the heavens; he explained that desire is defiling and gives rise to all manner of faults, and that if craving does not arise, the mind is immediately freed from hindrances.
At that time, the king and his retinue, having heard this Dharma, all gave rise to pure faith; they took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and received and upheld the precepts.

They then conceived toward the World-Honored One a mind of peace and happiness, a supple mind, a supreme mind, a mind free from hindrances, a mind without attachment, and a mind of virtuous compliance.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the king and the assembly had their minds opened and their intentions liberated, further proclaimed for them the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—using countless skillful means, according to the teaching methods employed by previous Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

At that time, the king and the assembly did not rise from their seats, yet they were all able to fully comprehend the principles of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. They saw the Dharma and knew the Dharma; they attained the pure Dharma, the equal Dharma, the firm Dharma, the stable Dharma, the non-resentful Dharma, the indestructible Dharma, and the non-falling Dharma. Just as white cloth easily takes on dye, so too did the king and his followers obtain this great benefit.

At that time, the king and his retinue, having been granted the essential points of the Dharma by the Buddha and having been shown profit, benefit, and joy, rose from their seats and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.

At that moment, there were guardian deities of the void, guardian deities of seeds, guardian deities of national boundaries, guardian deities of undertakings, guardian deities of grass, guardian deities of wood, guardian deities of livestock, guardian deities of forests, and guardian deities of roads. All these deities spoke in human voices and said to one another:
“The World-Honored One possesses great supernormal powers and great majestic might; he is able to perform various miraculous transformations and such deeds.”
He then spoke these verses:
"Today King Bimbisāra, together with his retinue, has taken refuge in the Buddha;
Having heard the Dharma and gained benefit within the Bamboo Grove, We deities as well shall take refuge in the Buddha."
At that time, King Bimbisāra, together with his retinue, circumambulated the World-Honored One to the right and departed from the assembly.
Furthermore, in Rājagṛha there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Sañjaya, who dwelt therein with his own followers.
After Śāṇakavāsin had passed away, his two disciples— one named Śāriputra and the other named Mahāmaudgalyāyana—
abandoned that community and said to one another:
"If either of us two first attains some realization, we must certainly inform the other."

Later, on one occasion, the Venerable Upasīna, having dressed himself in his robes and taken up his alms bowl at the time for eating, entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food from house to house in sequence.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing the Venerable One approaching from afar with his faculties stilled and his deportment composed and dignified, thought to himself:
"The deportment and movements of this Venerable One are rare and most supreme."
Having reflected thus, he approached him and asked:
"Venerable sir! Who is your teacher?"
"What further teaching did he speak?
Upasena replied, "My teacher is that Great Śramaṇa;
amidst the great assembly, he definitively proclaimed the Dharma-gate of the vast and great power of invincibility."
Śāriputra said: "Could you now, for my sake, proclaim from that Dharma-gate, whether briefly or at length? Upacina replied:
"What my Teacher has taught is the doctrine of dependent origination.
As for the phenomenon of dependent origination, it means that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, and cease from causes and conditions."
Furthermore, with this meaning, he spoke these verses:
Whatever phenomena arise through causes and conditions, Those very phenomena cease through causes and conditions.
This principle of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions Was taught by the Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, Śāriputra was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. He then spoke these verses:
"These wondrous phrases on dependent origination, The Venerable One has skillfully revealed to me.
Throughout nayutas of eons, I have neither seen nor heard them; today I have encountered them."
Having spoken these verses, he further said:
"Venerable One! Where is the World-Honored One now?"
Upasīnā replied, “The World-Honored One is currently at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery.
She spoke again:
"May I now go to the presence of the World-Honored One? He replied,
"You may do as you wish."
At that time, Śāriputra recalled the previous agreement made with Mahāmaudgalyāyana and thought, "I should now go to inform him. Having reflected thus, he went at once.
When Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw Śāriputra’s deportment and majestic bearing, which were superior to what they had been before, he knew that Śāriputra must have realized the Dharma.
He then said to Śāriputra, "Have you attained some realization?"
Śāriputra said: “The Dharma of dependent origination taught by the Blessed One was briefly explained to me by Upasīna, which I have realized. As it is stated in the verse he spoke:
‘Whatever phenomena arise through conditions, Those same phenomena cease through conditions.’”
"This is the causal condition for arising and ceasing, as taught by the Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa.
Having heard this Dharma, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Kāśyapa and the other great śrāvakas, as well as all the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and accepted it with faith.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Part One, Scroll Lower.
